descripcion_es: Nouns that name ideas, processes and qualities.
resumen: Formal abstract nouns (rationale, framework, trade-off, outcome) that let you talk about ideas precisely. They are the basis of the nominal style of reports, essays and presentations.

explicacion.texto: Formal English condenses ideas into nouns: instead of “because prices went up, people bought less” you write “the rise in prices led to a decline in consumption”. Mastering these nouns, with their prepositions, gives you precision and register.

filas: rationale (for)
the underlying reason or justification (es: justificación, razón de fondo)
The rationale for the reform is clear.
framework
a basic structure of rules or ideas (es: marco)
The EU provides a legal framework.
trade-off (between)
a balance between competing goals (es: disyuntiva, compromiso entre objetivos)
There is a trade-off between growth and stability.
outcome
the final result (es: resultado, desenlace)
The outcome of the vote is uncertain.
shortcoming
a fault or weakness (es: deficiencia, carencia)
The report highlights several shortcomings.
drawback
a disadvantage (es: inconveniente)
The main drawback is the cost.
feasibility
how possible or practical something is (es: viabilidad)
They studied the feasibility of the project.
accountability
the duty to answer for your decisions (es: rendición de cuentas)
Citizens demand greater accountability.
sustainability
the ability to continue over time (es: sostenibilidad)
The sustainability of public finances.
awareness
knowledge that something exists or matters (es: conciencia, conocimiento)
There is growing awareness of the issue.
reliance on / dependence on
the state of depending on something (es: dependencia de)
Europe's reliance on imported gas.
shift (in / towards)
a change of direction (es: cambio, giro)
A shift towards renewable energy.
scope
the range covered; room for action (es: alcance, margen)
The scope of the study is limited.
bias
an unfair tendency or distortion (es: sesgo)
The survey shows a clear bias.
insight (into)
a deep understanding; a revealing idea (es: comprensión profunda, idea reveladora)
The book offers insight into Roman life.
assumption
something accepted as true without proof; a starting hypothesis (es: supuesto, hipótesis de partida)
The model rests on several assumptions.
commitment (to)
a promise or obligation you accept (es: compromiso (con))
Their commitment to reform is weak.
willingness / reluctance (to)
being ready / unwilling to do something (es: disposición / reticencia (a))
There is reluctance to raise taxes.
leverage
power to influence or put pressure (es: influencia, palanca)
Small states have little leverage.
consistency
coherence; regularity (es: coherencia, regularidad)
The policy lacks consistency.
resilience
the ability to recover quickly (es: resiliencia, capacidad de recuperación)
The resilience of the banking system.
hindsight
understanding of an event after it has happened (es: perspectiva a posteriori)
With hindsight, the decision was a mistake.

items: Pay attention to the preposition: reliance ON, insight INTO, commitment TO, rationale FOR, shift TOWARDS.
Many are uncountable (awareness, accountability, leverage): no “a” and no plural.
“Consistent” = coherent; it does not mean Spanish “consistente” (solid, which is “solid” or “substantial”).

ejemplos.frase: With hindsight, we should have left earlier.
ejemplos.traduccion: Visto ahora, deberíamos habernos ido antes.

ejemplos.frase: The main drawback of living in the centre is the noise.
ejemplos.traduccion: El principal inconveniente de vivir en el centro es el ruido.

ejemplos.frase: Her novel offers real insight into family life in the 1950s.
ejemplos.traduccion: Su novela permite comprender de verdad la vida familiar en los años cincuenta.

ejemplos.frase: There is still some reluctance to accept the new rules.
ejemplos.traduccion: Todavía hay cierta reticencia a aceptar las nuevas normas.

ejemplos.frase: The coach praised the team's resilience after the defeat.
ejemplos.traduccion: El entrenador elogió la capacidad de reacción del equipo tras la derrota.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The dependence of foreign energy is a risk.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Dependence on foreign energy is a risk.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The building's foundations are very consistent.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: The building's foundations are very solid.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “consistente” (solid, firm) is “solid”; “consistent” means coherent or constant.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: We need a bigger conscience of the problem.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: We need greater awareness of the problem.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “conciencia” of something is “awareness”; “conscience” is your moral sense.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The compromise of the government with the reform.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: The government's commitment to the reform.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “compromiso” in the sense of an obligation you accept is “commitment”.

ejercicios.frase: Europe must reduce its reliance ___ imported energy.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the central idea of the card: each abstract noun is learnt with its fixed preposition, and the list of Rules and key points recalls “reliance ON”. The clue is the noun “reliance” itself, which comes from the verb “rely on” (depend on, trust) and keeps its preposition. That is why the correct sentence is “its reliance on imported energy”. Spanish says “dependencia de”, and that “de” is exactly what pushes you to choose “of”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Europa debe reducir su dependencia de la energía importada.

por_opcion.on: Correct: “reliance on” and “dependence on” always take “on”, just like the verbs “rely on” and “depend on”.
por_opcion.of: Incorrect: it is a calque of Spanish “dependencia de”. In English “reliance of” would only appear to show who depends (“the reliance of Europe on gas”), never what you depend on.
por_opcion.from: Incorrect: “from” shows origin (“energy from Russia”), but it is not the preposition that goes with “reliance”.
por_opcion.in: Incorrect: “in” does not combine with “reliance”; it appears with other nouns such as “a shift in” or “a rise in”.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a noun (understanding after the event).
ejercicios.frase: With ___, it is easy to see what went wrong.
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the noun “hindsight” from the table, “understanding after the event”, which almost always appears in the fixed phrase “with hindsight” or “in hindsight”. The clue is the rest of the sentence: “it is easy to see what went wrong” describes what you understand once you already know the result. “Hindsight” is uncountable, so it takes no article and no plural. It is the opposite of “foresight”, which would be the ability to see it beforehand.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “With hindsight” = looking back after the event.
ejercicios.traduccion: Visto a posteriori, es fácil ver qué salió mal.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Perspective” is a point of view in general; for “seen now, after the event” English uses the fixed phrase “with hindsight”.
“Hindsight” is uncountable: it does not take the article “a”.
“Foresight” is the ability to anticipate; here we are talking about understanding after things have happened.

glosario.significado: perspectiva a posteriori; «with hindsight»: visto ahora, a toro pasado
glosario.definicion_l: understanding the nature of an event after it has happened

ejercicios.frase: There is always a ___ between flexibility and security.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is “trade-off (between)”, which the table explains as a balance between competing goals: gaining in one means giving up part of the other. The clue is “between flexibility and security”, two competing goals, and the preposition “between”, which goes with “trade-off”. The correct form is “a trade-off”, a countable noun with a hyphen. It is a key term in economics: every policy involves “trade-offs”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Trade-off” = a balance between two competing goals.
ejercicios.traduccion: Siempre hay una disyuntiva entre flexibilidad y seguridad.

por_opcion.trade-off: Correct: a balance between two competing goals; it takes “between”.
por_opcion.trade-in: Incorrect: a “trade-in” is a used item given as part of the payment for a new one (for example, your old car when you buy another).
por_opcion.trade-up: Incorrect: “to trade up” is to exchange something for a better or more expensive version; it does not express a trade-off.
por_opcion.tradeoff of: Incorrect: the spelling “tradeoff” without a hyphen exists (mainly in American English), but “of” is unnecessary, because “between” already follows.

glosario.significado: disyuntiva, compromiso entre objetivos que compiten
glosario.definicion_l: an exchange that occurs as a compromise
the property of being flexible; easily bent or shaped · the quality of being adaptable or variable

ejercicios.frase: The campaign aims to raise conscience of the risks of smoking.
respuestas: The campaign aims to raise awareness of the risks of smoking.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is one of the false friends on the card: Spanish “conciencia” of a problem is “awareness”, whereas “conscience” is your moral sense (the inner voice that tells right from wrong). The clue is the collocation “raise … of the risks”: what a campaign increases is public knowledge, and the fixed phrase is “raise awareness of”. The correct sentence is “The campaign aims to raise awareness of the risks of smoking”. “Awareness” is uncountable, so it takes no article.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “concienciar” is “raise awareness”; “conscience” is your moral sense.
ejercicios.traduccion: La campaña pretende concienciar sobre los riesgos de fumar.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The campaign aims to raise conscience of the risks of smoking.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: “conscience” is your moral sense, not knowledge of a problem.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The campaign aims to raise consciousness of the risks of smoking.
errores_previstos.explicacion: “Consciousness” is being awake or collective awareness in a philosophical sense; the usual collocation for campaigns is “raise awareness of”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The campaign aims to raise an awareness of the risks of smoking.
errores_previstos.explicacion: “Awareness” is uncountable in this fixed phrase: you say “raise awareness”, with no article.

glosario.definicion_l: motivation deriving logically from ethical or moral principles that govern a person's thoughts and actions · conformity to one's own sense of right conduct

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a noun (the duty to answer for your decisions).
ejercicios.frase: Voters are demanding more transparency and ___ from their leaders.
ejercicios.explicacion: The word required is “accountability”, which the table explains as the duty to answer for your own decisions to others. The clue is its partner in the sentence, “transparency”, with which it forms a very frequent collocation in political language, and the verb “demand from their leaders”. It is uncountable, so it takes no article after “more”. It comes from the adjective “accountable” (“to be accountable to voters”).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Accountability” = the duty to answer for your decisions (es: rendición de cuentas).
ejercicios.traduccion: Los votantes exigen más transparencia y rendición de cuentas a sus dirigentes.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Responsibility” is responsibility in general; the idea of having to explain yourself and answer to others is “accountability”.
It is uncountable in this sense: it has no plural.
“Accounts” are financial or bank accounts; Spanish “rendición de cuentas” is not translated word for word.

glosario.definicion_l: responsibility to someone or for some activity
permitting the free passage of electromagnetic radiation · the quality of being clear and transparent

ejercicios.frase: The book gives us a fascinating ___ into the mind of a genius.
ejercicios.explicacion: It is “insight (into)”, which the table defines as a deep understanding or a revealing idea. The decisive clue is the preposition “into”, which the card highlights as the fixed partner of “insight”: you get inside something to understand it from within. Hence “a fascinating insight into the mind of a genius”. None of the other words is built with “into”.
ejercicios.traduccion: El libro nos ofrece una visión fascinante de la mente de un genio.

por_opcion.insight: Correct: a deep understanding of something; it takes “into”.
por_opcion.outlook: Incorrect: “outlook” is the prospect for the future or your attitude to life (“the economic outlook”, “a positive outlook”), and it takes “on” or “for”.
por_opcion.overview: Incorrect: “overview” is a general view or summary (“an overview of the topic”), the opposite of going deep, and it takes “of”.
por_opcion.sight: Incorrect: “sight” is the sense of vision or something you see; it does not mean understanding.

glosario.significado: comprensión profunda de, visión reveladora de

glosario.definicion_l: someone who has exceptional intellectual ability and originality · unusual mental ability

ejercicios.frase: The government reaffirmed its commitment ___ the climate goals.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule of fixed prepositions: the card recalls “commitment TO”. The clue is the noun “commitment”, in the sense of an obligation you accept, which comes from “to be committed to”. Spanish says “compromiso con”, and that is why the typical mistake is to use “with”. Note also that “compromise” is not a commitment, but a concession or a middle-ground agreement.
ejercicios.traduccion: El Gobierno reafirmó su compromiso con los objetivos climáticos.

errores_previstos.explicacion: It is a calque of Spanish “compromiso con”; in English “commitment” takes “to”.
“For” goes with other nouns on the card (“rationale for”), but not with “commitment”.
“Commitment of” would show who commits, not to what; here you need “to”.

ejercicios.frase: Before investing, they carried out a ___ study.
ejercicios.explicacion: The word is “feasibility”, and the fixed collocation is “feasibility study”. The clue is “Before investing”: before an investment you study whether the project can be carried out, technically and economically. In English the noun works here like an adjective in front of “study”, with no preposition. “Viability” exists, but the established phrase for this type of report is “feasibility study”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: A study of whether a project is viable is a “feasibility study”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Antes de invertir, realizaron un estudio de viabilidad.

por_opcion.feasibility: Correct: a “feasibility study” is the study done before launching a project.
por_opcion.possibility: Incorrect: “possibility” is the chance that something may happen; it does not name the analysis of whether a project can be carried out.
por_opcion.viability of: Incorrect: “viability” exists, but “of” breaks the structure, because “study” follows and there is no complement; besides, the usual phrase is “feasibility study”.
por_opcion.probability: Incorrect: “probability” is the numerical likelihood that something happens; it makes no sense here.

ejercicios.frase: The only ___ of the flat is that it has no lift.
ejercicios.explicacion: The word required is “drawback”, which the table explains as a disadvantage. The clue is the structure “The only ___ of the flat is that…”, which presents a specific downside of something that is generally good. “Downside” (more informal) and “disadvantage” (more neutral) are also accepted, because all three mean the same in this sentence. All are countable and are followed by “of”.
ejercicios.traduccion: El único inconveniente del piso es que no tiene ascensor.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Inconvenient” is an adjective (impractical, badly timed); here you need a noun.
“Inconvenience” is the trouble or discomfort caused to someone (“sorry for the inconvenience”), not the disadvantage of a thing.
“Shortcoming” is a lack or a defect in quality; for the downside of having no lift, the natural word is “drawback”.

glosario.definicion_l: the quality of being a hindrance
having a surface without slope, tilt in which no part is higher or lower than another · having a relatively broad surface in relation to depth or thickness

glosario.significado: ascensor (inglés británico; en EE. UU., elevator)
glosario.definicion_l: the act of giving temporary assistance · the component of the aerodynamic forces acting on an airfoil that opposes gravity

ejercicios.frase: There is a growing dependence of tourism in the islands.
respuestas: There is a growing dependence on tourism in the islands.
There is a growing reliance on tourism in the islands.
ejercicios.explicacion: It is the same case as “reliance”: the card recalls that “dependence / reliance” take “on”, and the first item in the list of typical mistakes is precisely “dependence of”. The clue is the noun “dependence”, derived from “depend on”. The correct sentence is “a growing dependence on tourism”; “reliance on”, which means the same, is also fine. Spanish “de” is not translated as “of”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hay una creciente dependencia del turismo en las islas.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There is a growing dependence of tourism in the islands.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: “dependence of” is a calque; you depend “on” something.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There is a growing dependence from tourism in the islands.
errores_previstos.explicacion: “From” is not the preposition for “dependence” either; the only correct one is “on”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There is a growing dependency of tourism in the islands.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Changing to “dependency” fixes nothing: the preposition is still wrong.

glosario.definicion_l: pass into a condition gradually, take on a specific property or attribute; become · become larger, greater, or bigger; expand or gain

ejercicios.frase: The model is based on the ___ that people behave rationally.
ejercicios.explicacion: The word is “assumption”, a starting hypothesis, very common when talking about economic models. The clue is “The model is based on the ___ that…”: what holds up a model is its assumptions, and “assumption” can be followed by a “that” clause. “Assumption” is countable and here takes “the” because it is specified in the following clause. Do not confuse it with “presumption”, which is more legal.
ejercicios.traduccion: El modelo se basa en el supuesto de que la gente se comporta de forma racional.

por_opcion.assumption: Correct: a starting hypothesis; it allows “the assumption that…”.
por_opcion.presumption of: Incorrect: “presumption” is used mainly in law (“presumption of innocence”), and “of” clashes with the “that” that follows.
por_opcion.assuming: Incorrect: it is a verb form; after “the” you need a noun.
por_opcion.consumption: Incorrect: “consumption” is the act of consuming; it looks similar because of the ending, but makes no sense in the sentence.

glosario.definicion_l: celebration in the Roman Catholic Church of the Virgin Mary's being taken up into heaven when her earthly life ended; corresponds to the Dormition in the…

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a noun (change of direction).
ejercicios.frase: We are seeing a major ___ towards remote work.
ejercicios.explicacion: The word required is “shift”, which the table explains as a change of direction and which is built with “in” or “towards”. The clue is “towards remote work”: there is a movement in one direction. “A major shift towards” is a very frequent collocation in the press. “Move” is also accepted, which in this context also means a movement towards something.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “A shift towards” = a change of direction towards.
ejercicios.traduccion: Estamos viendo un gran giro hacia el teletrabajo.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Change” is too general and usually takes “in” or “to”; “a change towards” sounds unnatural compared with “a shift towards”.
“Turn” is a turn in a physical sense or a change of course (“a turn for the better”), but it does not form the collocation “a major turn towards”.
“Tendency” is an inclination; what is described is a change under way, which is “shift”.

ejercicios.frase: Small countries have little ___ in international negotiations.
ejercicios.explicacion: The word is “leverage”, which the table defines as influence: the power to put pressure on others to get something. The clue is “little ___ in international negotiations”: “little” goes with uncountable nouns, and the card points out that “leverage” is one. That is why it takes no article and no plural. It is a term widely used in diplomacy and in finance, where it also means borrowing to increase returns (es: apalancamiento).
ejercicios.traduccion: Los países pequeños tienen poca capacidad de presión en las negociaciones internacionales.

por_opcion.leverage: Correct: influence or power to put pressure; it is uncountable, so it fits with “little”.
por_opcion.lever: Incorrect: a “lever” is the physical tool; it is countable and does not express negotiating power.
por_opcion.leveraging: Incorrect: it is the -ing form of the verb “to leverage” (to make use of); it does not work as a noun here.
por_opcion.leave: Incorrect: “leave” is permission to be away from work (“maternity leave”); it has nothing to do with influence.

glosario.significado: influencia, capacidad de presión; en finanzas, apalancamiento
glosario.definicion_l: the mechanical advantage gained by being in a position to use a lever · strategic advantage; power to act effectively
a discussion intended to produce an agreement · the activity or business of negotiating an agreement; coming to terms

ejercicios.frase: There was some ___ among members to accept the new rules.
ejercicios.explicacion: The word required is “reluctance”, unwillingness to do something, which the table presents together with its opposite “willingness”. The clue is the construction “___ … to accept”: “reluctance” is followed by “to” + infinitive. Also, “some” in front indicates an uncountable noun in this use. It corresponds to the adjective “reluctant” (“they were reluctant to accept”).
ejercicios.traduccion: Hubo cierta reticencia entre los miembros a aceptar las nuevas normas.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Reticence” exists, but in English it mainly means reserve when speaking, not unwillingness to do something; with “to accept” you use “reluctance”.
It is the adjective; after “some” you need the noun “reluctance”.
“Resistance” takes “to” + noun (“resistance to change”), not “to” + verb as here.

glosario.significado: reticencia a, falta de disposición a

glosario.definicion_l: one of the persons who compose a social group (especially individuals who have joined and participate in a group organization) · anything that belongs to a set or class

respuestas: The rationale for the reform is not clear
ejercicios.explicacion: The sentence revolves around “rationale (for)”, the underlying justification, with the preposition the card highlights: “rationale FOR”. The order is that of a normal English sentence: subject (“The rationale for the reform”) + verb “is” + “not” + adjective “clear”. The clue for telling the two “the” apart is the capital letter: “The” opens the sentence and the other goes before “reform”. The negation “not” always goes after “is”.
ejercicios.traduccion: La justificación de la reforma no está clara.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The rationale of the reform is not clear
errores_previstos.explicacion: Besides using a word that is not in the list, “rationale” takes “for”, not “of”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The rationale for the reform not is clear
errores_previstos.explicacion: The negation goes after the verb “be”: “is not”, never “not is”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Not is clear the rationale for the reform
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is the order copied from Spanish “no está clara la justificación”; in English the subject goes before the verb.

glosario.significado: justificación de, razón de fondo de

glosario.definicion_l: a change for the better as a result of correcting abuses · a campaign aimed to correct abuses or malpractices

descripcion_larga_es: Formal abstract nouns (rationale, trade-off, accountability, hindsight…) that formal English uses to condense ideas into a few words. They are essential for reading the economic press and reports and for writing or presenting precisely. They are difficult for Spanish speakers because of their fixed prepositions (reliance on, insight into) and several false friends (consistent, conscience, compromise).

contexto.que_es: These are nouns that name not objects but ideas, processes and qualities: the justification for a measure (rationale), the balance between two goals (trade-off), the duty to answer for decisions (accountability). Many are uncountable and almost all combine with a fixed preposition.
contexto.por_que_importa: Formal English prefers the nominal style: instead of linking clauses with because or so, it condenses the idea into a noun (“the rise in prices led to a decline in consumption”). Without this vocabulary a text sounds childish or vague, and in a C1-level oral or written exam it is what makes the difference in register. A misused false friend (consistent for Spanish “consistente”) also causes real misunderstandings.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: In reports, opinion articles, speeches, documents from international organisations and any reasoned presentation. The signals are contexts of analysis: advantages and disadvantages, causes, results, the assumptions of a model. Spanish speakers tend to copy the Spanish preposition (dependence of) or choose the false friend (conscience, compromise); it is best to memorise each word with its preposition.
